Health System—Funding
1. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Health :
What was core Crown health expenditure  as a percentage of GDP in 2010 -11 and what
is it in 2015-16?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The 2015 Financial
Statements of the Government of  New Zealand state that in 2010 -11 core Crown health
expenditure was 6.7 percent of GDP, and in 2015 -16 it is forecast to be 6.4 percent of
GDP. This Government has increased health spending by $4 billion while increasing
access to services for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, does a 0.38 percent decrease in Crown
health expenditure—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, you’re going to say it’s a decrease.  Oh, good on you,
Annette.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: —as a percentage of GDP, Mr Joyce—between the 2010-11 and
the 2015-16 years equate to $930 million less going into health if the spending level had
stayed the same; if so, when will he acknowledge that health expenditure has been cut?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What a silly question. It quite clearly has not
been cut, because it has gone up by $4 billion over the term of this Government. You
had better go and talk to your question writer.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table—[Interruption] This is a point of order, Mr
Speaker.

March 2016, compiled from data from Treasury that shows exactly what I outlined in
terms of core Crown health expenditure.

table that i nformation from the Parliamentary Library. Is there any objection? There is
none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
2. JACQUI DEAN (National —Waitaki) to the Minister of Finance : What steps
has the Government taken to move its books from an $18 billion deficit in 2011 back to
surplus?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has taken a lot of
steps, because before this Government’s first Budget in 2009 Treasury was forecasting
never-ending deficits and net debt blowing out to over 60 percent of GDP, over twice
the level that it currently is. This was because o f a combination of a financial crisis and
the huge spending built in by the previous Labour Government, which included no
consideration—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to the Minister. I have a point of order from Grant
Robertson.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You have ruled several times
in this House that Government questions from its own members to Ministers should not
be used to at tack the Opposition. That was a primary question being used for that
purpose.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not agree at all that the primary question was set down for that
purpose. It was to inform members of this House. It was a legitimate question that w as
accepted. There was a huge amount of interjection coming from two particular
members, and if the Minister then takes the opportunity to respond to that interjection,
that is legitimate as well.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Just to finish off the answer, in the last seven Budgets of this
Government the annual cost of new initiatives has averaged around $600 million. In the
seven Budgets up to 2009 the average cost of new initiatives was around $3 billion per
year.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What ar e the Government’s fiscal priorities now that it has delivered
on its election promise and made a surplus in 2014-15?
9370 Oral Questions 3 Mar 2016

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The focus now is on paying down debt. Governments have
previously been able to get on top of debt beca use they relied on tax revenue windfalls,
helped by 4 to 5 percent inflation, as occurred in the first decade after 2000. With
inflation now at 0.1 percent we cannot rely on fast -growing tax revenue to achieve debt
reduction. So we have to continue with ti ght management of our spending. We are
doing this by better management of the Government’s huge asset base of $250 billion,
and also addressing the long -term drivers of our biggest area of spending, and that is in
social services, health, education, welfar e, and justice through our programme of social
investment.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of his answer that his priority is paying down debt, is it
correct that he will not begin to pay down a single cent of debt until the 2020 -21
financial year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The measure of debt that we use, as previous Governments
have, is debt as a percentage of GDP. That is peaking about now, but, certainly, paying
off nominal debt will require quite strict fiscal discipline, because we cannot rely on
high inflation to deliver big bursts of tax revenue. We have actually got to do what
every household and business in New Zealand does, and that is work to the real income
that we can earn.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Has the Minister i dentified a level of surplus at which he will cut
taxes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Not a particular level of surplus —this Government has done
a tax switch in 2010, actually, when we had a deficit, because we were able to cover the
cost of income tax reductions with increases in GST and property taxes. The
Government is committed to moderate tax cuts over the next few years if fiscal
conditions allow, and we have yet to see whether fiscal conditions will allow it.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What benefits will paying down Government debt bring to New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Holding and paying down debt will allow New Zealand to
be resilient, particularly to changes in the global economy that might have a negative
effect on us. To do that we need to keep a tight rein on ineffective spending. If we can
pay down debt, we will also be in a better position to deal with long -term spending
pressures such as superannuation. Our current public pension costs around 5 percent of
GDP; by  2050 the cost will increase to 8 percent of GDP. But to keep that in
perspective, in the last 4 years we have managed to reduce Government spending as a
proportion of GDP from 34 to 30 percent. So the reduction in Government spending as
a proportion of GDP in the last few years has been greater than the projected increase in
national superannuation through to 2050.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What implications does a focus on paying down debt have on the way
the Government manages its books?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Now that the Budget is broadly in balance and there is a
stronger focus on debt, we are not so concerned about small positive or negative
fluctuations in the Budget balance. This is particularly true for the monthly Crown
accounts, the  next of which will be released tomorrow, because month to month the
accounts can fluctuate depending on timing effects. The Government manages the
books by getting better results from our spending. That is, we are willing to spend more
where we can get re sults, but if we cannot get results, then we are not willing to spend
money—for instance, on large -scale new tertiary education entitlements, because there
is no evidence that that will make any difference to anybody.
3 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9371
Housing, Rental—Warrant of Fitness
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister for Building and

items.speaker: Housing
items.text: Does he stand by all his answers to Oral Question No. 1 in the House
yesterday?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, particularly my
answer pointing out how the Government’s insulation and smoke alarm requirements
will save 21 lives a year and the fact that our Government has invested $500 million in
making our homes warmer, drier, and safer —16 times what the previous Government
spent.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it not a fact that he misled the House yesterday when he claimed
that 18 lives would be saved through the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill, when,
in fact, the evidence is those lives would be saved by a much higher standard of
insulation and a range of other safety measures, including a heating device?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SM ITH
items.text: I stand by the numbers yesterday. They are provided in an
economic analysis research report, in which it said “ The health -related benefits arise
primarily from the retrofitting of insulation … A reduction in mort ality was the largest
benefit—preventing 18 deaths per year  …”. That is a report that was commissioned
independently from my ministry, and I stand by it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table two reports that show the connection between
the 18 deaths and a higher standard of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We need just the title of the reports and the dates.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: The first of those reports is the Cost Benefit Analysis for a Minimum
Standard for Rental Housing, from November 2014.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And the second?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: The second report is The Impact of Retrofitted Insulation and New
Heaters on Health Services Utilisation and Costs, Pharmaceutical Costs and Mortalit y,
from October 2011.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I just wan t confirmation that they are not readily available for
members if they want them.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I found them on the internet; they could be publicly available.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If they are publicly available, then members can source  them for
themselves.

items.speaker: Dr Parmjeet Parmar
items.text: Why does the Government not support the housing warrant
of fitness bill proposed by the member?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Government is not supporting the bill because it goes
too far; it is impractical. It would make it an unlawful act to rent or use a property that
does not have glass visibility strips and security stays on all windows. I know my own
private home in Nelson does not comply; I suspect the houses of most members of this
House would not comply. I do find it ironic that the Greens would compel glass
visibility strips on the windows of all other people’s buildings, but actually do not even
have them in Bowen House. It is that classic policy from the Greens—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We do not need that part to the answer.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I seek leave of the House to have a photo of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not —[Interruption] Order! The Minister will resume
his seat if he wish es to stay to answer the balance of the questions. I remind Dr Nick
Smith that when I rise to my feet and call for order, that is the time for him to resume
his seat. I do not want to have to remind him of that again.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Minister saying that it is silly and petty to have glass visibility
strips on windows and doors in rental homes when ACC reports that 133 children are
9372 Oral Questions 3 Mar 2016
injured by either falling through a closed glass window or out of a window every week
in this country; more than 500 children a month injured?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: If that member truly believed that glass visibility strips
should be on all windows, I simply challenge her why she does not have them in her
own office? If the member really believed that was a practical requirement to impose on
every building owner in New Zealand, she could start by setting a good example.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister apologise to this House for misleading New
Zealanders by claiming that 18 lives would be saved by his bill when all of the evidence
that he has referred to and has been tabled in the House shows that those 18 lives would
be saved only by a much higher standard of insulation, and a clean -heating device, than
what is required in his bill?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, because the member is wrong. I can quote directly
from the analysis. It says: “ The health -related benefits arise primarily from  the
retrofitting of insulation …”. It goes on to quote the  reduction in mo rtality that would
occur, the benefits of hospitalisation, and the reduction in pharmaceutical costs. They
are exactly the things the Government is doing. What we are not going to do is to have a
pedantic warrant of fitness that will impose costs of admini stration alone of over $100
million, and which, actually, most members of this Parliament’s own private homes
would not comply with.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does his advice not go on to say that the research on those 18 lives is
based on an insulati on standard as at 2008 —a much higher standard than the miserable
1978 standard in his bill? Why will he not tell the whole story?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Because the member misunderstands both the bill and the
regulations that the Government  has put forward. New Zealand did not require
insulation in homes that were newly constructed until 1978. What our bill and
regulations require is that if a home has no insulation, you will be required to install
insulation as per the current standards.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, the current standards —that is very clear in the
regulations. What the Government is not going to do is to have someone who put
insulation in their house in 2010 now having to rip  it out and put stuff in that meets the
current standard. It is exactly the sort of approach that we would take in, for instance, an
area with earthquake -prone buildings where there is a different standard for those
buildings that are new, but that does no t necessarily mean it makes sense to require
absolutely every building in New Zealand to meet new building standards.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it not also the case that the Grimes report the Minister tabled on
Tuesday said that with a higher stand ard of insulation and a heating device, older New
Zealanders with respiratory illness would gain an additional 4 years of life through
those two measures—neither of which are in his bill?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I would, firstly, draw the member’s attention to the existing
housing regulations that make reference to the requirements around heating devices.
The second is simply this—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did specifically refer to the
Grimes report—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question. What we need to do is allow the
Minister the courtesy to respond to the question. If the Minister then does not answer
the question, let us have a look at the matter then, but at least allow the Minister to get
more than 10 or 12 words out before we can address whether he has addressed the
question or not.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: And the bit the member does not seem to understand is that
if we imposed a requirement on every landlord  in New Zealand to provide a new heat

pump today, that is a cost that you impose on the sector that would ultimately be passed
on in rents. There are not free goods when you have a regulatory cost that is passed on,
and that is the part that the member seems to be ignorant of.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Point of order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am just going to invite the member to repeat the question,
because I know what the point of order will be. Would the member please repeat the
question for the benefit of the Minister.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it not true that the Grimes report, which the Minister tabled in the
House on Tuesday, said that with a higher standard of insulation and a heating device,
older New Zealanders with respirator y illness would gain an additional 4 years of life
based on those measures—neither of which are in his bill?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: First, the member is mistaken. The report that I tabled from
Mr Arthur Grimes earlier in the week was solely on the issue of home insulation, not on
the issue of heating, and in that respect the member is incorrect.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is the Minister making up numbers and misrepresenting the
research to show his bill does better than it will when  all he needs to do is improve the
standard of insulation in the bill to make sure that New Zealanders’ lives will genuinely
be saved through this measure?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The confusion of the member is confirmed by that very
question, in that the bill does not set the level of regulation that is in the bill. That is set
in the regulations, and the regulations make plain that for new insulation being installed,
it needs to meet the modern standard, but that it would be unreason able for someone
who has an insulation standard that was built in the 1990s to have to rip that out to meet
some sort of pedantic requirement, for which the Greens, unreasonably, would impose
costs on the sector. Those costs are ultimately passed on in ren ts and hurt the very
people whom we were attempting to help.
Tourism—Economic Contribution
4. SCOTT SIMPSON (National—Coromandel) to the Minister of Tourism: What
reports has he received about the contribution tourism is making to the economy?
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Associate Minister of Tourism)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Tourism
items.text: I have more good news for touri sm. The latest International
Visitors Survey shows that international tourist spending has increased by an
outstanding 31 percent to $9.7 billion in the year to December 2015. This confirms that
the tourism sector’s focus on increasing both value and volum e is working. Tourism is
now worth $10.6 billion —or nearly 5 percent of GDP —and is our second -largest
export.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: How has the Government’s investment in tourism promotion helped
grow the sector?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENN ETT
items.text: This Government’s unprecedented $700 million
investment in tourism and tourism promotion is working to attract tourists from our key
markets. So total spending by visitors from China is up 63 percent to $1.6 billion, and
from the United States is up 4 0 percent to $1 billion. Tourism New Zealand has put
together some very innovative and highly targeted campaigns and social media
campaigns. Australian model Megan Gale is the face of the new social media campaign
to promote the New Zealand cycle trails, in Australia, our largest tourism market.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What role is increased airline capacity playing in getting more
visitors to come to New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: It may surprise you that that means more visitor s coming
to New Zealand because we have more flights —who would have thought! Just today
Air New Zealand —[Interruption] Thank you. Just today Air New Zealand has
9374 Oral Questions 3 Mar 2016
announced it was resuming seasonal flights between Osaka and Auckland, with Japan
being our fif th-largest tourism market. This comes on top of our new routes to the US
and Argentina. There are also now direct Emirates flights between Auckland and Dubai,
making it easier to get here from Europe. New flights between New Zealand and China,
Indonesia, and Malaysia have also been announced this year. On the regional front, of
course, Jetstar is making a huge difference in our domestic market. The good news
around tourism both domestically and internationally is outstanding for our country and
its economy.
KiwiSaver—Employer Contributions
5. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Revenue
items.text: Does he stand by all of his answers to Oral Question No. 4 yesterday?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yes, with one small
correction. When I said, as evidence of my concern to ensure all contributions were
passed on to KiwiSaver acc ounts, that there was a 99.994 percent collection rate, I
should have said a 99.94 percent collection rate.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: When he said, yesterday, that he had been unable to verify media
reports that 46,154 people had not had their emp loyer contributions paid to their
KiwiSaver accounts, did he realise that information came directly from his department?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yes, I was aware of those reports as having
originated from the Inland Revenue Departmen t (IRD). I am now advised that the
46,000 number provided by IRD does not represent the number of employees who have
not had KiwiSaver employer contributions passed on. It represents the number of
KiwiSaver employees of those employers who may not have pas sed on all of the
contribution. So it is a rather nuanced difference —the number of actual people affected
by that is less than that and, in the time available, IRD has not been able to provide the
exact number. That should not detract from the fact that IR D, and I, remain very
concerned to ensure high levels of compliance.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: To assist the Minister in the House, I seek leave of the House to
table information released by the Inland Revenue Department earlier this year—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it available on their website?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: No, as far as I am aware, it is not. It includes a table of the total
number of employees who have not had employer contributions deducted from their
account.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular document. Is there any
objection? [Interruption] Order! There is objection —there is objection. Order! I put the
leave, there was objection. That is the end of the matter. If the member now wishes to
continue his supplementary questions, I invite him to do so.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How does the Inland Revenue Department identify those
companies that are failing to pass on employer contributions to KiwiSaver accounts,
currently numbering 2,210 companies, and what intervention measures does it take?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: The first sign of any non-payment is usually with
the employer schedules that transfer payments like PAYE, ACC levies, and KiwiSaver
contributions. When  that occurs, the Inland Revenue Department has a range of
interventions that start with follow -up calls and conversations about whether or not
there are cash-flow issues or technical difficulties that prevented the physical payment.
As a consequence of that, the overwhelming majority of those payments are remedied in
a short period of time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he therefore satisfied that the Inland Revenue Department is
performing that role correctly, when there are still 46,000 New Zealanders who have not
got in their KiwiSaver account what they are entitled to?
3 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9375

11. MARK MITCHELL (National —Rodney) to the Minister of Trade : What

Pacific Partnership, and what further consultation will occur?

behalf of the  Minister of Trade : The consultation process for the Trans -Pacific
Partnership (TPP) has been amongst the most extensive that a New Zealand
Government has undertaken for any trade negotiation, with hundreds of meetings taking
place across the negotiating process, as well as public submissions. The Government
has made available a large amount of documentation, including the full text of the
agreement, detailed fact sheets, and the national interest analysis. For all of this year the
TPP will receive extensive parliamentary and public scrutiny. The legislation will be
considered by the select committee for the full 6 months, allowing a significant amo unt

items.text: Starting next Monday the Government is running a
series of nationwide roadshows on the TPP. The roadshows are for intereste d members
of the public to learn more about this important trade agreement and to assist businesses
to identify and plan for the new export opportunities when the TPP comes into force.
Roadshows are being held in Auckland, Christchurch, Dunedin, Wellington , Hamilton,
Napier, Nelson, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Tauranga, and Whangarei. There
will also be a number of hui to discuss with iwi and Māori businesses the outcome of
the TPP negotiations, as well as the huge opportunities for Māori to benefit fro m the
TPP.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: How will the TPP create significant new trade opportunities for
New Zealand companies?

items.text: The TPP is New Zealand’s biggest -ever trade deal,
providing access to our exporters to  more than 800 million consumers, across 11
countries. These countries account for 36 percent of the global economy, and include
the largest and the third -largest economies in the world: the United States and Japan.

agreement partners once the TPP is fully phased in. In total, the TPP will ultimately
represent $274 million a year in tariff savings, which is around twice the savings
initially forecast for the China free -trade agreement. The TPP supports our exporters to
grow and create new jobs, and to diversify their business overseas. Not being in the TPP
would put the New Zealand economy and our businesses at a competitor’s
disadvantage.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I have to say that when I
completed the first part of my speech the other night, we were thoroughly enjoying this

9382 Radiation Safety Bill 3 Mar 2016
to amend an old Act that is 50 years old and was in desperate need of overhaul —
something that started with a review a long time ago when I was the Minister of Health.
That was 11 years ago, although you would think it was just yesterday. So it was time to
review and update the Act.
When I was last speaking, I had just started a little explanation as to why we needed
to change the name of the bill from the Radiation Safety Bill to one that really did tell
you what this bill was about. I wanted to change it so that it was the “Ionising Radiation
Safety Bill” because at the select committee there was no doubt that there was some
confusion between what was ionising radiation and what was non -ionising radiation.
The members of the committee were very fortunate that we were well served by some
superb officials from the Ministry of Health, who were able to lead us through the
explanation as to what the differences were —although I must give credit to Kevin
Hague, who probably understood a little better than most.
We were led through the differences and understood what we were doing, but my
concern and why I wanted the Government to change the name so that it was more clear
was that I do not believe that many of the public know what, in fact, we are legislating
for. This would have made it very, very obvious. What we were not passing legislation
to regulate was non -ionising radiation, and this is t hings like your cellphone towers,
your Wi-Fi, and your microwave ovens and ultraviolent tanning machines —although I
have to say that that is another debate we will have at a later date, and why we are not
regulating them out of existence, I do not know, bu t they are not included in this bill. It
does not include your power lines, although some people think that they are included.
So it was a great disappointment that the Government did not accept a name change,
and I know that the members of the Health Comm ittee, including my colleagues in the
National Party, would not have minded that change because they knew that there was
confusion in the public’s mind about this. But, you know, in the way that this place
works, it did not happen, and so we now have a Radiation Safety Act coming into place.
It is going to update our legislation, as I said. It is going to bring us into high -level
compliance with international best standards and also with our commitments to
international treaties. That is pretty important, and long overdue.
So Labour supports this bill. We are pleased to see it come to its conclusion 50 years
after it was first passed, and after many, many years of it being reviewed and looked at.
I want to say that I think that the members of the select comm ittee worked extremely
hard on this bill. We came back to this House with a bill that I think is fit for purpose —
maybe not for the next 50 years, because, as has been pointed out, a lot of technology
has changed in that time. There are some members on our select committee who can
remember when there was not television, but there was also—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Only that member.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Well, I will not name them, but there are some who can
remember it.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Don’t name yourself.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Mr Bishop, of course, would not remember it because he,
in fact, remembers hardly any of the modern appliances. So—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I just love this, but unf ortunately the member’s time has
expired.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): It is becoming quite a habit to follow
after the Hon Annette King. I am particularly pleased that Labour and, I b elieve, all
parties are supporting this bill in the House.
The Radiation Safety Bill, today in its third reading, is a relatively simply piece of
legislation by its nature, but complex in its details. I say it is relatively simple because
as a piece of legislation it really is here to do two things. One is just to update the
3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9383
domestic regulations, structures, and operations —the logistical elements, if you will —
of how we deal with radiation, and we will come to the whole ionising and non -ionising
element in a moment. There is the domestic side that the bill seeks to update, and then
there is the international side.
Just to touch on the international side quickly and briefly. New Zealand, in so many
ways, has chosen to oblige itself with a variety of interna tional agreements on a whole
lot of things. One of them is around the likes of radiation and the management of
radiation. As has been pointed out by other speakers in this debate and in the past, the
current radiation safety Act—or, as it is actually known, the Radiation Protection Act—
was passed in 1965. The treaties that were about and other things have changed since
then, and so this bill brings us into line with international agreements. It is something
that we as a Parliament are required to do, if you  will, if we are going to maintain those
relationships. Importantly, too, it means that we will accord ourselves with the various
principles of the agencies. Some of them are monitored through the UN. So that is quite
important.
I will just state for the r ecord that this bill does not affect the nuclear -free legislation
of New Zealand or any of the disarmament Acts. That sometimes gets raised with me
and others, but this bill is dealing with ionising radiation, and what we are talking
about—think of the lik es of magnetic resonance imaging and think of X -rays. That is
the sort of area that we are talking about.
We are also talking a lot of things medical. Most radiation sources in New Zealand
are down two sides, or two camps. One is research. If you go into any of the universities
of New Zealand there will be radiation sources, often used in the science departments
and the medical departments. The second area where you will find a lot of devices, and I
think there are about 4,500 licences —in other words, 4,500  instances where radiation
sources are able to be used. The other big player, bar research, is medical. So,
obviously, there are the scanning technologies, and often technologies for the treatment
of various cancers. Brachytherapy comes to mind, and ionise d or radiated metal balls
that are used in order to destroy cancers. You have ionised iodine often used for the
likes of thyroid cancers and so forth. So that is what we are talking about there.
There has been plenty of debate, and some part of me—a very small part of me—will
miss the constant discussions in the Health Committee about ionising and non -ionising
radiation. None of us are nuclear physicists, but I have to say after all those discussions
I feel far more comfortable about the distinction now —but it is only somewhat tongue -
in-cheek when I say that I will miss those ongoing discussions. Look, I am not going to
get into the science of it, but, needless to say, with the advice that we are given and
which I and I think all members understand, the dis tinction is very, very clear between
things, and also in the nature of the examples that are given. We heard it from the
previous speaker, Annette King. You know, the likes of non -ionising radiation—we are
talking about the likes of sunbeds and Wi -Fi and p ower poles and so forth, OK? It is
quite a distinct difference between that and the irradiating of metal objects as in
brachytherapy and so on.
So we understand why, and I think it is important for people out there to understand
as well that just because this bill does not cover the likes of power lines and Wi -Fi and
the like does not mean that there are not regulations and guidance around it. There is
plenty of that through other legislative measures. That is quite positive in and of itself.
The select co mmittee itself was very constructive. I think we realised very early on
that we were, at one level, out of our depth here in the scientific knowledge. But one of
the great things about select committees is that we actually have two ears, two eyes, and
one mouth, and we used those, I think, exceedingly well to listen, see, and speak to the
officials. So once again I want to acknowledge their work and advice and, speaking
9384 Radiation Safety Bill 3 Mar 2016
personally, acknowledge them for actually taking sometimes very complex ideas and
breaking them down in a way that I could understand. I think that helped us, as a
committee, move forward. I think what we have done was very collegial and, as
previous speakers have indicated, has brought a very good bill back to this House.
In concluding, beca use we have spoken on this many, many times, I just want to
touch on a few of the changes that the select committee brought forward. One really
important one is particularly for users in medical fields, dental and otherwise. We put in
a new clause to say that, basically, if someone has a licence they can have someone else
work under their supervision. OK, there are a few nuances around that, but basically, if I
were to read it, an unlicensed user can use a radiation source while they are under the
direct supervision of someone else. So, again, licences must be given to someone who is
going to use the radiation source. Ionised iodine and brachytherapy treatments —as long
as the source user and the holder of the licence has given permission, then someone else
is able to be guided through that process.
For those who are military minded, be absolutely assured that the legislation, as
proposed here at the third reading, does not prejudice the rights of national security or,
therefore, of our defence forces. There a re other rules that assist there. Also,
importantly, initially in the bill we just talked about enforcement officers. We did go
through that quite carefully to make sure that people understood that the likes of the
police, chief fire officers, and others c an have some jurisdiction in this space if
something was to go wrong.
Finally, the importance of codes of practices has been written into the bill, and that
links me back to where I started, which is around the whole thing of how this is
updating our inter national obligations. In doing so, we were able to tap into
international best practice, which informs our codes of practice. So this is a good bill. It
has been worked on very well by the Health Committee. I think we can be very happy
with the progress of this bill, and I commend it to the House, title and all.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: It is my turn to take a call on
the Radiation Safety Bill. As the previous speaker s have discussed, one of the key
discussions, really, has been around the ionising and non -ionising radiation.
Unfortunately, I did not have the privilege of sitting on the Health Committee at the
time when the discussion happened, so I actually took the o pportunity to inform myself
about the difference between ionising and non -ionising radiation. And I looked to the
World Health Organization for a definition. The definition that it provides is “ Ionizing
radiation is radiation with enough energy so that dur ing an interaction with an atom, it
can remove tightly bound electrons from the orbit of an atom, causing the atom to
become charged or ionized.”
It has been a long time since science class, so I have done some further exploration
of that, and it is really  around electromagnetic radiation. The impact of ionising
radiation when it binds with electrons in the orbit of an atom is that it actually causes
the structure to change, which is the ionisation of it. There is a continuum, I guess —a
spectrum around the energy where you have low -frequency use at one end and high -
frequency use at the other end. So at the low -frequency end we are talking about things
like radio waves, microwaves, infrared, and visible light. At the higher end we are
talking about X -rays and  gamma rays. For the purposes of this bill, we really are
specifically talking about X -rays and gamma rays. So that is what I understand is the
context within the Radiation Safety Bill —that is the nub of the issue, so to speak. Not
all electromagnetic radi ation is ionising, as I say. It is, generally, just the X -ray and
gamma-ray end of the spectrum.
One of the examples that I think it would be useful for the House to think about is
when you are having X -rays at the dentist before you are having treatment. The dentist
3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9385
will ensure that they are well protected in the use of the X -ray machines. As I
understand it, there was a discussion around who was licensed or authorised to use the
piece of equipment that has the radiation source within it. Generally speakin g, in a
dental practice it will be the lead dentist who will have the licence and they may, under
supervision, allow other members of their staff to use the equipment, but it would be
with some specific criteria around that use. That is as I understand it,  and I think that
has been confirmed by the members of the select committee who did hear the evidence
from the officials. It would have been an interesting discussion for those who are
scientifically minded, because I understand that from schedule 2, for e xample, there
would have been a really lively discussion around concentration levels and the activity
and the source, and if you are anything like me, the periodic table is back there in the
mists of time. So I really acknowledge that. In relation to the t echnical ability for this
bill there would have been some real opportunity for the officials to support the select
committee members in their understanding of this particular topic.
The legislation itself does some other things. It allows New Zealand to b ecome
compliant with the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear
Terrorism and the Amendment to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear
Material, and the protection of nuclear material, I guess, in practical terms, is t he
example that I quoted around the dentist. It also covers the transportation, disposal, and
use of that material. And I want to pay particular reference to cobalt -60, which is used
in irradiation of food —particularly of materials that come through our bo rders that
might have pests or other material on them that could pose a biohazard to New Zealand
and have an impact on our agriculture and our export of products.
It also allows for international inspectors to be appointed and to undertake activities
in New Zealand through the International Atomic Energy Agency. It provides a regime
for the authorisation of individuals and organisations using radiation materials. So here,
again, I am referring to, for example, dentists who may use X -ray machines in the
course of their treatments, and those people whom they supervise to use those pieces of
equipment. It provides within the bill the penalties for contravening these authorities.
For an individual, that fine could be up to $100,000, and for an organisation it co uld be
The director is appointed by the Minister of Health, who then administers a register
of those contracted sources —those who are using the radiation in their equipment. The
director will also appoint inspectors, who can seize a radiati on source to prevent or
mitigate any risk. I referred to cobalt -60 previously. That, I understand, caused some
discussion, particularly around the radiation of food products, and there was some
discussion that was held at the select committee about that. I  refer to schedule 2, “List
of radioactive material and acceptable activity concentration levels and activity levels”,
and also schedule 3, “Dose limits for ionising radiation”, whether that be through
occupational exposure or through public exposure.
As I said, I did not have the privilege of being on the Health Committee at the time
that the bill was under discussion. I think I would have enjoyed the opportunity to do
some scientific work; I did not have the opportunity to do that. I know that the
committee is well considered and I acknowledge the hard work that it has done on this. I
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: It is a pleasure to
speak on the third reading of the Radiation Safety Bill, and I would like to begin by
congratulating Poto Williams, the previous speaker, because she obviously did not have
the opportunity that we had to listen to the wonderful explanations that the officials
gave us, but I thought she gave a wonderful account. So I say thank you very much to
the previous speaker.
9386 Radiation Safety Bill 3 Mar 2016
The Radiation Safety Bill is about establishing a modernised framework to protect
the health and safety of people and the environm ent from harmful effects  around
radiation. As other speakers have said, it will bring New Zealand into line with
international best practice. It is modernising an Act that is 50 years old. I have very
vivid memories of being a new member of Parliament, wal king into my office, and my
executive assistant saying to me “Today, Barbara, you’ve got to speak for 10 minutes
on radiation.”, and I thought: “Oh, OK.” So the first thing I did was, I went to
Wikipedia, but it did not make any more sense to me after that . Of course, we have had
a lot of discussion since then about ionising and non -ionising radiation, but at that stage
it did not make any sense at all.
The thing that really struck me about this bill at the time —and I remember the aspect
that I took from it was the fact that the Act was 50 years old. It was interesting to me to
note at the time that that was when The Sound of Music  was released and it was also
about when the Beatles released their song “Yesterday”, and I know we have had
previous speakers ta lking today about the introduction of television. Well, I cannot
remember the introduction of television as such, but I can remember the introduction of
colour television, which was a very exciting time.
I remember when we first started debating this bill in the House, we were having
conversations about mince pies, microwaves, and all sorts of things in an effort to
understand this whole picture of radiation. Then, I have to say, it was fantastic because
when the officials came in we were presented with som e excellent information and
some excellent, clear graphs and charts that made the process of working through this
piece of legislation much, much clearer. Even though I did a little bit of biology,
chemistry, and physics at school, the presentations we had —although they have not
made me a scientist —have given me a much clearer understanding of the process of
ionising and non-ionising radiation.
But I think it is important to remember, as we, as members of Parliament, enact some
of these pieces of legislatio n, that our primary role in this is to ensure that the piece of
legislation is going to achieve what it sets out to achieve, and our role is to assess the
situation to see whether it really is going to protect our people from the harmful effects
of radiation. We all know that in the last 50 years we have come a long way. We are all
carrying around devices. We have got things in our homes: the technology, the
internet—the things we never ever dreamt about have come such a long, long way, and
so has radiation. So it is important to realise that these changes will help us in providing
better and more modern health services. So, as was mentioned before, X -rays and the
like are a big part of this, there is also quite an element of this involved in dentistry, and
these changes are going to help us do this more safely and will protect our public.
It will also protect the environment, because when we have people in hospitals who
are having X-rays, it is not only the person who has the X -ray who is exposed but it is
the people who stand in the room or in the corridor just making sure that we have got
the right standards in place so that not only the patient is safe but all of those people
around them are very safe. I have to say that we have made great advances with ca ncer
treatment in the last few years, and cancer radiation and chemotherapy waiting times are
now at world gold standard. So it is really important to realise that not only are people
getting a better, quicker service but now this legislation will be prote cting them even
further than it did before.
It is also important that the select committee has asked to insert a new clause, which
is clause 92A, and that requires the Director of Radiation Safety to review each code of
practice once every 5 years. So I t hink for me, looking at a piece of legislation that has
been on the table for 50 years, it is really important that with the advances in technology
3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9387
we are making now, those things are looked at and the Director of Radiation Safety will
actually be active over each 5-year period to make sure that this does not drag on.
So it is a real pleasure to be speaking on this bill today. I do want to commend the
officials again, and I also want to say it is wonderful to be working as part of the Health
Committee, under the chairmanship of Simon O’Connor and with the members whom
we have in this group. We have worked extremely well together over time, and it is a
pleasure to commend this bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: I rise to give what will be my final contribution on this
bill, and, actually, the Greens’ only contribution in this debate today. As several other
speakers have commented, I think that the officials from the ministry did a really terrific
job of working with the Health Committee on this pretty technical subject, and they
were praised highly in the debate on the second reading, but they deserve praise in this
debate also.
Simon O’Connor, in his contribution, remarked on the fact that th is bill effectively
has two purposes: first, to bring New Zealand into line with our international
obligations under the International Atomic Energy Agency and, secondly, to modernise.
Barbara Kuriger has just referred to the fact that this is legislation that is 50 years old. I
guess there is nothing like legislation that touches on science to expose, fairly brutally,
how legislation can become out of date. Certainly, the legislation that we are replacing
is obsolete legislation. I wonder sometimes whether  there may be some value in having
some sort of systematic review of old legislation so that other Acts —like, for example,
the Adoption Act 1955, which is also well past its use -by date—could also be reviewed
by this House.
I think the debates in the House  on this matter, and at the select committee, have
focused to quite a considerable degree on this business of whether or not the bill should
cover not only ionising radiation but also non -ionising. Several speakers in this debate
have referred to that. The  original recommendation from officials was that the bill
should cover both —that all forms of radiation should be regulated through this
particular statute. There is certainly some sense to that. Poto Williams, in her
contribution—even though she did not p articipate in the debate in the select
committee—I think had it right when she talked about there being a continuum of
energy that radiation could potentially possess, and the difference between the amount
of energy that something needs to ionise and that which would not be enough to ionise
it. The boundary is just a hair’s breadth. There actually is a continuum, but in practical
terms there is more of a difference.
Officials told us, first of all, that for non -ionising radiation we have regulation that
has been kept more up to date. As new devices become available, regulation has been
put in place that has, in fact, protected the public from potential harms, although I think
Annette King is completely right to draw the House’s attention to a bill that we ha ve yet
to finish debating that really covers an area —namely, sunbeds and solaria —where a
source of non -ionising radiation is able to produce the kinds of serious harms that are
perhaps more worthy of the kind of strong regulation that this bill provides for.
The regulation of non -ionising radiation has been kept more up to date than the
statute on which we rely for the safety of ionising radiation. I guess too that the
qualitative effects are significantly different. Perhaps with the exception of the sunbed s
and solaria example, non-ionising radiation is typically stopped and absorbed within the
skin, and it is within the skin that any adverse effects are likely to be felt, whereas
ionising radiation will typically penetrate the skin and cause havoc within t he body by
ionising cells within it. Those particles that are produced by that ionisation process will
go on to damage DNA, causing either direct harm or, potentially, mutation that will
9388 Radiation Safety Bill 3 Mar 2016
cause harm down the track. Both practically and in terms of effects, there are
distinctions that can be reflected in different types of regulation.
There are, none the less, some odd effects that come about from having different
regimes for dealing with the two types of radiation. I have referred in earlier
contributions in  the House to the fact that in a hospital, for example —and other
speakers have, quite rightly, referred to the fact that it is in health care settings that
many of these forms of radiation crop up —literally within the same radiology
department, one will have a magnetic resonance imaging suite and technology that uses
a form of non-ionising radiation that is regulated in a different way from what may be in
the next room, and the X -ray machine in the next room will be regulated by this bill.
There is an admin istrative inefficiency that is created by having different regimes for
dealing with the two. It is a difficult balancing act, I guess, to get this right.
Although at the beginning of this process I felt that both forms of radiation should
probably be regu lated by this bill, on balance I think that it is reasonable to have
separated the two. None the less, the level of confusion among the public that exists
around the distinction between these two forms of radiation and the subtlety of the
difference, I thi nk, would have justified support for the change to the name of the bill
proposed by Annette King. I believe that the bill we are passing into law today ought to
have been called the “Ionising Radiation Safety Bill”.
I close by making reference to something  that I think is probably always worthy of
note when the House is debating a bill that has scientific implications, and that is the
matter of scientific literacy. The submissions that the committee received were small in
number, and mostly from people with  expertise in the field. Some of those submissions
were extremely useful, but one or two of the submissions reflected a misunderstanding
of the science, and I know that in some of the more general comments that existed in the
community about this bill, such misunderstanding of the science was also present.
I worry that the internet —one of those technical apparatus, shall we say, that has
come into existence in the 50 years since the original Act was passed —has meant that
people have access to an extraordina ry amount of information, and that information
varies very widely in its quality, from very helpful and authoritative information at one
end through to information that is misleading and unhelpful at the other.  That has
created a situation where New Zealan ders, perhaps more than ever before, need to be
able to discern the difference between the two —to know, when we look at something
that is on Wikipedia, for example, or that is found on some other website, whether the
information there actually has scientif ic validity. If we do not possess that science
literacy, then we will draw conclusions that are invalid, and the contribution that we can
then make to the debate about scientific matters in this country is compromised.
I close by supporting the bill, but a lso supporting the House’s doing what it can to
improve scientific literacy. Thank you.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I am very pleased to rise on behalf of New
Zealand First in the third reading of the Radiation Safety Bill. I was very pleased to be a
part of the Health Committee as we reviewed the submissions and talked with the
officials, who made sure that our knowledge was far greater than it was when we first
started looking at this bill. Non e of us are medical physicists, and we needed that
particular help.
I was very interested in Kevin Hague’s speech —we can always learn in this
particular area. I would like to say a big thankyou to the officials for their patience,
particularly as we all came up to speed.
We support this bill. We know that it is for the safe use of ionising radiation. This
bill will repeal and replace a very outdated Act, the Radiation Protection Act. It is long
overdue. There have been a lot of scientific developments in th e 50 years since this bill
3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9389
was first introduced, and it is important that our legislation keeps up to date with the
latest technology, particularly in this age. On this occasion, we believe that the New
Zealand public will be reassured that the bill will b ring our legislation into line with
international best practice and the principles of radiation safety. We are also satisfied,
too, that the dose limits for radiation exposure are consistent with international
standards, and there have been a number of sta ndards, which were read out by previous
speakers, that we needed to bring our legislation in line with.
We were pleased to hear that there is now a legislative provision for the registration
of radiation sources. Previously, only licence holders were requi red to be registered.
This bill ensures that we now have provisions that are required by the International
Atomic Energy Agency code of conduct. As other people have already pointed out, it is
good to see that the penalty for offences against the legislati on are going to be
increased. We definitely need deterrents in this part. For this bill, it definitely
successfully balances the benefits of ionising radiation with the health and safety of
people and the environment.
All of us on the select committee were  very aware of the concerns that were voiced
to us regarding non -ionising radiation. We are very satisfied that these two regulations
should remain separate from this bill, hence our desire to see the title changed. It is far
easier to identify what legisl ation one is looking at when we have “Ionising Radiation”
or “Non-Ionising Radiation” in the title. We are quite satisfied now that we are at this
point.
Although the bill proposed that it will be voluntary for applicants for a source licence
to submit a radiation safety plan, we believe it should be compulsory for every applicant
for a source licence to submit a radiation safety plan for safety, security, and
emergencies. That plan should identify how the individual or organisation is going to
comply with the requirements of the bill.  We believe that this is essential to ensure that
the Act is actually complied with. One of the areas that we have some concerns about is
that we want to hear how the Government is planning on supporting operators so that
they themselves are fully prepared for the changes that have been made to this
legislation.
In conclusion, we believe it is a very necessary bill, which ensures our regulations
are aligned with international best practice and the principles of radiation safety.
Therefore, New Zealand First is very happy to support this bill in its final reading, and
we will follow its implementation closely. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I am happy to als o, with other members
around the House, endorse the Radiation Safety Bill in its third reading, and note that
this is another piece of legislation that is being brought up to date to reflect current
medical applications —not only for medical uses but also f or uses in veterinary
medicine, industry, and research. This is a bill on which the House has worked
cooperatively—the Health Committee has worked cooperatively.
I do note the suggestion that this bill could have had a different name. However, this
is the Radiation Safety Bill, and if we remember the purpose of this bill, it is indeed to
reflect modern practice and modern safety levels with the use of radiation in its many
applications, which are mostly to the betterment of people in our excellent health
system. With those few words, I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, here we are —finally we get to the third reading
of the Radiation Safety Bill. I have had the privilege, I think, o f speaking on every
single reading of this bill, despite the fact that I was not on the Health Committee, and
was not able to hear any of the—

items.text: The member was robbed.
9390 Radiation Safety Bill 3 Mar 2016

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Robbed of being on the select committee. You are quite right—it
was a select committee that I had been on in another term of Parliament, but not during
this one. So I did not get the benefit of the advice from the officials, but I take the
members’ word for it that the officials should b e thanked for the very good information
they provided during the deliberation on this important bill, because it does bring us up
to speed.
I have had it suggested to me that the reason I have been on the speaking list every
time on this bill is that my ow n children have broken enough bones to have enough X -
rays that I should know enough to speak on the bill on this matter. I just want to dispel
that myth to start off with. Yes, there has been the odd time that my boys have been
robustly playing their chose n game that they are passionate about —basketball—and
they may have ended up having X -rays. But the problem has not necessarily been the
issues associated with this bill, but this: could the Government please bring a bill before
the House that would stop bo nes being broken on statutory holidays? That is the
problem I have had—every single bone that has been broken in our household seems to
happen on a statutory holiday, and that is when you have to pay the most to actually get
the bone X-rayed. So if you can fix that please, I would very happy.
But that is not what this bill attempts to do, and neither should it. It is actually a bill
that brings New Zealand’s practice up to speed with international best practice. I do
want to support what the Green member Ke vin Hague raised in his contribution. It
would be good to think that we had a process in place so that when Acts become out of
date when technology and our scientific knowledge has moved on, to the extent that we
know about dangers that we once did not kno w about, there would be some automatic
scrutiny of Acts that ensured we did not just have to wait for some Minister’s office to
notice that the Act had become horribly out of date or for something to go badly wrong
before we realised that such an Act had become out of date.
The last time this Act had attention was 50 years ago. I think in one of my previous
contributions to this debate I may have said that it has been as long in the making as I
have been on this earth-ish, because I never declare my actual age, but I am sure people
can go and look that up for themselves. I mention this because the technological
advances and the scientific knowledge that we have made over the course of my lifetime
explains to me the reason why I am a little worried that it to ok so long before we
reviewed this Act again, and perhaps we should have processes in place to ensure that
we do that in a more timely fashion. None the less, we are here now.
This bill does repeal and replace the Radiation Protection Act 1965. So, in fact , the
Act is a little younger than I am —a little younger. One purpose of the bill is to enable
New Zealand to meet its international obligations under a range of international treaties
relating to radiation protection, radiation safety and security, and nu clear non -
proliferation. That is important, because New Zealand has —not always —on many
occasions led on non-proliferation of nuclear issues, and so it is rather surprising that we
have taken so long to update this legislation.
Labour does acknowledge the n ecessity of updating legislation such as this in order
to keep pace with the technological advances and changes. Annette King tried to amend
this bill to change the title of it so that it was more correct, because the legislation that
we are debating does not cover all forms of radiation. In fact, it covers only the ionising
radiation form. So those are the ones that we are familiar with when X-rays are taken.
I guess, alongside accompanying my children for X -rays from time to time —not too
regularly—that the other time that I come across X -rays and the use of them is when I
go to the dentist. Is that not a bit disconcerting when you are having an X -ray taken at
the dentist, and everyone else in the room bolts while you sit there and have the X -ray?

items.speaker: I often do sit there and think
items.text: “Gosh, should I be bolting as well? Is the harm that can be
3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9391
omitted that bad that all of the other people in the room are dashing before they go
somewhere and push the button remotely?”. In times gone by, people such as the dentist
and the dental technician would have stayed there and they would have been in the same
environment. But, of course, what we now know is that regular exposure —not the
irregular exposure of me having an X -ray once in a blue moon, but the regular
exposure—of t hose workers in their workplace to that health and safety hazard is no
longer acceptable, and so we have these new systems in place to deal with this.
So on the one hand our health and safety legislation in the workplace has kept apace
of these changes, bu t this Act, which we are amending today when we are debating the
Radiation Safety Bill, has not kept apace in the same way. We do support having a high
level of compliance with international best standards, and we do support our
commitments to international treaties.
The bill does cover not only the use of ionising radiation but the transportation and
the disposal of ionising radiation, both man -made and naturally occurring, in quantities
above stated levels. The fundamental requirements stipulate that radi ation use occurs
only where the expected benefit outweighs the risks, that exposures must be kept as low
as reasonably achievable, and that prescribed dose limits must not be exceeded. So these
are important factors when we think about the fact that it is our children who are
exposed to this ionising radiation and that it is older people who are frequently exposed
to these, because probably they are the two groups who are most exposed to X-rays over
the course of their lives. So it is very important that th ey are protected with that
statement.
The enactment of the bill will complete New Zealand’s domestic implementation of
the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism and the
Amendment to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material. It allows
for the International Atomic Energy Agency international inspectors to be appointed by
the director to undertake activities in New Zealand, and international inspectors must be
accompanied by an enforcement officer appointed by the director under clause 39 of the
bill. So it introduces a new regime of authorisations for individuals or organisations
using radiation materials. [ Bell rung] I was anticipating this being a split call, but no
other member wants to share t he call with me, so I think at this stage I will just simply
reaffirm that Labour supports this bill and commend it to the House.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Before making some v ery brief

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Tēnā koe e Te Māngai o Te Whare. I too

This law reform actually completes New Zealand’s domestic implementation of,
firstly, the International Convention for the Suppression of A cts of Nuclear Terrorism.
We actually signed that convention on 14 September 2005, so today we will actually
join 101 other nations to now ratify this convention in our domestic legislation. It also
completes our commitment to the Amendment to the Conventi on on the Physical
Protection of Nuclear Material, which was adopted on 8 July 2005, and, again, that
ensures that our domestic legislation now puts us in that group of countries that have
taken the convention seriously, and our domestic legislation now re flects that

This law reform enables us to meet our international obligations relating to radiation

3 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9393

items.text: I rise with the final call on this bill to

9394 Employment Standards Legislation Bill 3 Mar 2016
Second Reading
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): I move, That the Employment Standards Legislation Bill be now read a second
time. I thank the members of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee and its
chair, Jonathan Young, for their hard work and consideration of the bill. I want to also
add my thanks to the hard -working officials providing support both to the committee
and to me behind the scenes. I think they have done an excellent job. I also want to
thank all those who made submissions on the bill. The bill has come back from select
committee in very good shape. The select committee has recommended that the bill
proceed with some amendments, which I am in support of.
Although much of the public discourse on the bill has been about zero -hour
provisions, this bill does much more than address that issue, and I want to touch on
those matters first. There are very important changes to paid parental leave included in
this bill, which deliver on my party’s 2014 election promise to modernise and extend
paid parental leave.
Part 1 of the bill remains  largely as it was at introduction, although the committee
has made some useful changes that will improve the clarity of the bill. The definition of
“primary carer” has been tightened to ensure there is no misinterpretation. A primary
carer, if not the bio logical mother or her spouse or partner, is a person who takes
permanent primary responsibility for the care, development, and upbringing of a child
who is under the age of 6 years. The outlined provision in Part 1 has also been revised
in response to feedback from some submitters about the complexity of the bill.
I also requested that the committee consider the proposal to extend the parental leave
payments for parents of pre -term babies, following discussion with ACT leader David
Seymour. The proposal ref lects the extra and unexpected time the parents spend in the
hospital with the baby and away from work, and the delay in establishing bonding and
settling the baby into the home environment. The committee agreed that eligible persons
should receive an addi tional week’s parental leave payment for each week of
prematurity, from 37 weeks, and additional keeping -in-touch hours, the extra paid
parental leave up to an additional 13 weeks. I want to thank Mr Seymour for his
contribution to this very important amendment.
Part 2 of the bill amends the Employment Relations Act. The changes introduce
broad new accountability provisions around knowingly and intentionally committing
breaches of employment standards, measures improving record -keeping requirements,
and the overturning of the statutory obligation on the Employment Relations Authority
and the Employment Court to send employment standards cases to mediation. No
substantive changes have been made to Part 2 of the bill but, again, the committee’s
consideration of submitters’ comments has led to minor improvements in their clarity
and workability. Legislative guidance has been added to clarify how to meet the new
requirement to have a record of both the hours worked each day and the pay for these
hours. This requirement is necessary for the correct calculation of, and demonstration of
compliance with, minimum employment entitlements. Some other minor changes have
been made to the provisions, overturning the statutory obligation on the Employment
Relations Authority to send employment standards cases to mediation.
I want to turn now to the provisions to address what are known as zero -hour
contracts. These attracted the most comment from submitters. Most submitters opposed
the proposals, particularly relating to avai lability provisions, on the grounds that they
believed they legitimised the very practices the bill attempts to stop. This is quite
wrong, in my view. It does, however, underscore the difficulty that arises when there is
3 Mar 2016 Employment Standards Legislation Bill 9395
no clear definition or shared under standing about what zero -hour means. Zero-hour is a
type of employment that requires the employee to be ready, willing, and available for
work when work is offered. Sometimes this obligation is paired with an exclusivity
clause that also prevents the emplo yee from working for others, even when the
employer has little or no work to offer. It is the equivalent of being on call all the time,
without being paid anything to recognise the demands that poses.
This is distinct from casual employment, where there is  neither obligation on the
employer to offer work nor obligation on the employee to accept it. Casual agreements
have been a part of the employment relations landscape in this country for a long time.
Some in this House may be concerned at the increasing c asualisation of the workforce,
but these changes are not aimed at eliminating casual agreements, which I believe have
a place in our employment relations landscape.
A number of the submissions highlighted a range of ways we could better achieve
these obje ctives. In my view, the committee has taken a sensible and pragmatic
approach to the concerns raised by submitters, and the bill is in better shape for it.
Under the amendments, employers must have a genuine reason, based on reasonable
grounds, to include an availability provision—that is, a provision requiring an employee
to be available for work. It must be in the employment agreement, and must provide
reasonable compensation for that availability. The bill provides guidance to employers
and employees on both of these requirements. Compensation for shift cancellation will
also have to be reasonable, and the bill provides guidance on this as well. The
committee has also clarified the provisions relating to wage deductions by adding that if
an employment agr eement contains a general consent to a wage deductions clause, the
employer must consult with the employee when the employer wants to make a specific
deduction. Finally, to give employers more time to make the necessary changes to the
employment agreements , particularly those employers with large workforces, the
original 6 -month transitional period to amend existing individual employment
agreements is extended to 12 months.
After the committee reported back to Parliament, there was a strong backlash from
some, who claimed that rather than eliminate zero -hour provisions, the bill had
entrenched them. I absolutely disagree with that assessment but felt that, for all the
hyperbole, the gap between where we were and those views was not as large as the
drum-beating would suggest. So, after discussion with the Council of Trade Unions and
others, I am prepared to make further minor changes to the clauses around availability
and the definition of reasonable notice, to close that gap. I acknowledge the input of the
Council of Trade Unions and also that of Iain Lees -Galloway, and note that Labour has
publicly indicated that, with those changes, it can support the bill through its remaining
stages. The changes made to the bill—

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: Let me be absolutely
clear. Labour does not support this bill in its current form. As it was reported back from

9396 Employment Standards Legislation Bill 3 Mar 2016
submitters, representing both workers and employers, we were not able to get the

eliminate zero-hour contracts, rather than entr ench them in the law. When the bill was

withdrawing our support for it. We do not believe that it gets rid of zero -hour contracts.
In fact, we believe it entrenches zero-hour contracts. Nothing has changed so far.
What has changed is that the Minister has reached out to us —I suspect because he
needs to make sure he has the numbers to pass this bill. The minor parties certainly were

Marama Fox in particular for the open line of communication that she allowed between
myself and the Māori Party. I would like to thank Peter Dunne for noticing when we
came out so hard against the bill when it was reporte d back from the select committee.
We have been in discussions with the Minister, and I thank the Minister for approaching
us and being prepared to discuss the issues that we have with this legislation.
So in good faith —because we on this side of the House believe in negotiating in
good faith—we will support the second reading of the bill. Nobody should interpret that
as Labour intending to support the bill through its remaining stages, until we have seen
the proposals. We have not yet seen the final proposa ls. We have certainly seen some
indication about where the Minister wants to go. We are happy with the direction that
the Minister has indicated he wants to go, but we have not seen the final proposals. So
until we see the final proposals we cannot commit to supporting this bill through its
